title: Bayesian Statistics: written exam
instructions: Answer **all five** questions (100 marks in total, about 120 minutes). Write your answers in LaTeX: use $...$ for inline maths and `\begin{align} ... \end{align}` for displayed derivations. Marks are given for the working, not only for the final answer. Unless told otherwise, give numerical answers to 3 decimal places (or as exact fractions). Standard facts about the Gamma, Beta, Dirichlet and normal distributions may be quoted; any other result must be proved or is stated in the question. The macros `\E`, `\Var` and `\Prob` are available in your answers.

questions.title: Normal and Weibull-Gamma models, Jeffreys and power priors
questions.text:
Lifetimes $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ are conditionally i.i.d. given $\lambda>0$ with the Weibull density (shape $k>0$ known)
$$f(y\mid\lambda)=k\lambda\,y^{k-1}e^{-\lambda y^{k}},\qquad y>0,$$
so that $\Prob(Y>y\mid\lambda)=e^{-\lambda y^{k}}$. Part (a) is a separate warm-up on the normal model; parts (b)-(e) use this Weibull model. The prior is $\lambda\sim\text{Gamma}(a,b)$ with shape $a$ and rate $b$, $\pi(\lambda)=\dfrac{b^{a}}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}$. Write $s=\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_i^{k}$. For $\text{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$ the mean is $\alpha/\beta$, the mode is $(\alpha-1)/\beta$ if $\alpha>1$, the variance is $\alpha/\beta^{2}$, and $\int_0^\infty\lambda^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta\lambda}\,d\lambda=\Gamma(\alpha)/\beta^{\alpha}$.

parts.text: *(Warm-up, separate from the Weibull model.)* Let $X_1,\dots,X_m\mid\theta\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(\theta,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2$ known, and prior $\theta\sim\mathcal N(\mu_0,\sigma^2/\kappa_0)$ with $\kappa_0>0$. Show that $\theta\mid x\sim\mathcal N\Big(\dfrac{\kappa_0\mu_0+m\bar x}{\kappa_0+m},\,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{\kappa_0+m}\Big)$, explain why $\kappa_0$ is called the prior pseudo-count, and prove that the posterior predictive distribution of a new $\tilde X$ (conditionally independent of $x$ given $\theta$) has variance $\sigma^2\big(1+\frac1{\kappa_0+m}\big)$.

markingScheme.step: Collects terms in $\theta$: coefficient of $\theta^2$ is $-(\kappa_0+m)/(2\sigma^2)$, of $\theta$ is $(\kappa_0\mu_0+m\bar x)/\sigma^2$; completes the square to obtain the stated normal
Explains pseudo-count: the posterior is what $m$ data points plus $\kappa_0$ extra observations equal to $\mu_0$ would give (precision $\kappa_0/\sigma^2$ is that of $\kappa_0$ observations)
Law of total variance: $\Var(\tilde X\mid x)=\E[\Var(\tilde X\mid\theta)\mid x]+\Var(\E[\tilde X\mid\theta]\mid x)$

parts.modelAnswer:
Up to a constant in $\theta$,
\begin{align}
\log\pi(\theta\mid x)&=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^m(x_i-\theta)^2+\kappa_0(\theta-\mu_0)^2\Big]\\
&=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\Big[(\kappa_0+m)\theta^2-2(\kappa_0\mu_0+m\bar x)\theta\Big]+\text{const}\\
&=-\frac{\kappa_0+m}{2\sigma^2}\Big(\theta-\frac{\kappa_0\mu_0+m\bar x}{\kappa_0+m}\Big)^2+\text{const}.
\end{align}
So $\theta\mid x\sim\mathcal N\big(\mu_m,\sigma^2/(\kappa_0+m)\big)$ with $\mu_m=\frac{\kappa_0\mu_0+m\bar x}{\kappa_0+m}$. This is exactly the posterior we would get from a flat prior and $m+\kappa_0$ observations, $\kappa_0$ of which equal $\mu_0$: the prior is worth $\kappa_0$ pseudo-observations.

For the predictive, $\E[\tilde X\mid\theta]=\theta$ and $\Var(\tilde X\mid\theta)=\sigma^2$, so by the law of total variance
$$\Var(\tilde X\mid x)=\E[\sigma^2\mid x]+\Var(\theta\mid x)=\sigma^2+\frac{\sigma^2}{\kappa_0+m}=\sigma^2\Big(1+\frac{1}{\kappa_0+m}\Big).\ \blacksquare$$

parts.text: Return to the Weibull model. Derive the posterior distribution of $\lambda$ given $y_1,\dots,y_n$, state its parameters and say in what sense the Gamma prior is conjugate.

markingScheme.step: Multiplies by the prior and drops factors not involving $\lambda$: $\pi(\lambda\mid y)\propto\lambda^{a+n-1}e^{-(b+s)\lambda}$
States $\text{Gamma}(a+n,\,b+s)$ (both parameters) and that prior and posterior lie in the same family (conjugacy)

parts.modelAnswer:
The likelihood is
$$p(y\mid\lambda)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}k\lambda y_i^{k-1}e^{-\lambda y_i^{k}}=k^{n}\Big(\prod_i y_i^{k-1}\Big)\lambda^{n}e^{-\lambda s}.$$
By Bayes' theorem, dropping every factor that does not depend on $\lambda$,
\begin{align}
\pi(\lambda\mid y)&\propto \lambda^{n}e^{-\lambda s}\cdot\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}\\
&=\lambda^{a+n-1}e^{-(b+s)\lambda},\qquad\lambda>0.
\end{align}
This is the kernel of a Gamma density, so $\lambda\mid y\sim\text{Gamma}(a+n,\;b+s)$. Prior and posterior both belong to the Gamma family, so the Gamma prior is conjugate to the Weibull likelihood with known shape.

parts.text: Take $k=2$, $a=2$, $b=1$, and suppose $n=5$ observations give $s=4$. Give the posterior distribution, the posterior mean, mode and standard deviation, and compute the posterior predictive survival probability $\Prob(\tilde Y>1\mid y)$ for a new lifetime $\tilde Y$ (conditionally independent of $y$ given $\lambda$). Show that $\E[e^{-t\lambda}\mid y]=\big(\beta/(\beta+t)\big)^{\alpha}$ when $\lambda\mid y\sim\text{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$. You may use part (b).

markingScheme.step: Writes $\Prob(\tilde Y>1\mid y)=\E[e^{-\lambda}\mid y]$ and proves the Gamma Laplace-transform formula by integrating the kernel

parts.modelAnswer:
By part (b) the posterior is $\text{Gamma}(2+5,\,1+4)=\text{Gamma}(7,5)$. Hence
$$\E[\lambda\mid y]=\frac75=1.4,\qquad\text{mode}=\frac{7-1}{5}=1.2,\qquad \text{sd}=\frac{\sqrt7}{5}\approx0.529.$$
For a new lifetime, $\Prob(\tilde Y>t\mid\lambda)=e^{-\lambda t^{k}}$, so
$$\Prob(\tilde Y>1\mid y)=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda}\,\pi(\lambda\mid y)\,d\lambda.$$
If $\lambda\mid y\sim\text{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$ then
$$\E[e^{-t\lambda}\mid y]=\frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^\infty\lambda^{\alpha-1}e^{-(\beta+t)\lambda}\,d\lambda=\frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\cdot\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)}{(\beta+t)^{\alpha}}=\Big(\frac{\beta}{\beta+t}\Big)^{\alpha}.$$
With $\alpha=7$, $\beta=5$, $t=1$:
$$\Prob(\tilde Y>1\mid y)=\Big(\frac56\Big)^{7}\approx0.279.$$

parts.text: (i) Find the Jeffreys prior for $\lambda$ in the Weibull model (shape $k$ known) and the posterior it gives. (ii) Let $\eta=h(\lambda)$ with $h$ strictly monotone and continuously differentiable. Prove that the Jeffreys prior is invariant under this reparametrisation: the Jeffreys prior computed directly in the $\eta$ parametrisation equals the density obtained by transforming $\pi_J(\lambda)$ to $\eta$. You may assume the score has finite variance.

markingScheme.step: (ii) Chain rule for the score: $\dfrac{\partial\log f}{\partial\eta}=\dfrac{\partial\log f}{\partial\lambda}\dfrac{d\lambda}{d\eta}$
(ii) Deduces $I_\eta(\eta)=I_\lambda(\lambda)\big(d\lambda/d\eta\big)^2$ (squares the score, takes expectation, $d\lambda/d\eta$ is not random)

parts.modelAnswer:
**(i)** For one observation, $\log f(y\mid\lambda)=\log k+\log\lambda+(k-1)\log y-\lambda y^{k}$, so $\partial^2\log f/\partial\lambda^2=-1/\lambda^2$ and $I(\lambda)=1/\lambda^{2}$. The Jeffreys prior is $\pi_J(\lambda)\propto\sqrt{I(\lambda)}=\lambda^{-1}$, $\lambda>0$, which is improper (the limit $a,b\to0$ of the Gamma prior). By part (b) with $a=b=0$ the posterior is $\text{Gamma}(n,s)$, proper whenever $n\ge1$.

**(ii)** Write $\lambda=h^{-1}(\eta)$. The score in the $\eta$ parametrisation is, by the chain rule,
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\log f(y\mid\lambda(\eta))=\frac{\partial\log f}{\partial\lambda}\cdot\frac{d\lambda}{d\eta}.$$
Square it and take the expectation over $y$ for fixed $\eta$; the factor $d\lambda/d\eta$ is not random, so
$$I_\eta(\eta)=\E\Big[\Big(\frac{\partial\log f}{\partial\lambda}\Big)^2\Big]\Big(\frac{d\lambda}{d\eta}\Big)^2=I_\lambda(\lambda)\Big(\frac{d\lambda}{d\eta}\Big)^2.$$
The Jeffreys prior built directly in the $\eta$ parametrisation is therefore
$$\pi_J(\eta)\propto\sqrt{I_\eta(\eta)}=\sqrt{I_\lambda(\lambda)}\,\Big|\frac{d\lambda}{d\eta}\Big|.$$
On the other hand, transforming the density $\pi_J(\lambda)\propto\sqrt{I_\lambda(\lambda)}$ to $\eta$ by the change-of-variables formula gives
$$\pi(\eta)=\pi_J(\lambda)\Big|\frac{d\lambda}{d\eta}\Big|\propto\sqrt{I_\lambda(\lambda)}\,\Big|\frac{d\lambda}{d\eta}\Big|.$$
The two expressions coincide, so the Jeffreys prior is invariant under reparametrisation. $\blacksquare$

parts.text: Historical data $x_1,\dots,x_{n_0}$ from the same Weibull model (same $k$) have $s_0=\sum_i x_i^{k}$. Starting from the improper prior $\pi_0(\lambda)\propto\lambda^{-1}$, construct the power prior with power parameter $\gamma\in(0,1)$, $\pi(\lambda\mid x,\gamma)\propto p(x\mid\lambda)^{\gamma}\pi_0(\lambda)$. Identify its distribution, and state its effective sample size when the ESS of $\text{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$ is defined as $\alpha$ (the number of pseudo-observations).

markingScheme.step: ESS $=\gamma n_0$: the historical data count as a fraction $\gamma$ of their size

parts.modelAnswer:
The likelihood of the historical data is $p(x\mid\lambda)\propto\lambda^{n_0}e^{-\lambda s_0}$, so
$$\pi(\lambda\mid x,\gamma)\propto\big(\lambda^{n_0}e^{-\lambda s_0}\big)^{\gamma}\lambda^{-1}=\lambda^{\gamma n_0-1}e^{-\gamma s_0\lambda}.$$
This is the kernel of $\text{Gamma}(\gamma n_0,\;\gamma s_0)$. Its effective sample size is $\gamma n_0$: the power parameter $\gamma$ discounts the historical sample, $\gamma=0$ ignores it and $\gamma=1$ counts it fully.

questions.title: Monte Carlo, inverse transform and importance sampling
questions.text: This question is about simulation-based estimation. Throughout, $U\sim\text{Unif}(0,1)$ and expectations are assumed to exist.

parts.text: Let $F$ be a continuous, strictly increasing cdf on its support with quantile function $F^{-1}$, and let $U\sim\text{Unif}(0,1)$. Prove that $X=F^{-1}(U)$ has cdf $F$.

markingScheme.step: Uses that $F$ is strictly increasing: $F^{-1}(u)\le x\iff u\le F(x)$

parts.modelAnswer:
For any $x$ in the support,
$$\Prob(X\le x)=\Prob\big(F^{-1}(U)\le x\big).$$
Since $F$ is strictly increasing, $F^{-1}(u)\le x$ holds if and only if $u\le F(x)$ (apply $F$ to both sides, or $F^{-1}$ to both sides). Hence
$$\Prob(X\le x)=\Prob\big(U\le F(x)\big)=F(x),$$
because $F(x)\in[0,1]$ and $\Prob(U\le c)=c$ for $c\in[0,1]$. So $X$ has cdf $F$. $\blacksquare$

parts.text: The Laplace distribution has density $f(x)=\tfrac12e^{-|x|}$, $x\in\mathbb R$. Derive its cdf and quantile function, and give the draws produced by inverse transform sampling from $u=0.2$ and from $u=0.9$ (3 decimal places).
parts.modelAnswer:
For $x<0$: $F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}\tfrac12e^{t}\,dt=\tfrac12e^{x}$, and $F(0)=\tfrac12$. For $x\ge0$: $F(x)=\tfrac12+\int_0^x\tfrac12e^{-t}\,dt=1-\tfrac12e^{-x}$.

Solving $F(x)=u$: if $u<\tfrac12$ then $\tfrac12e^{x}=u$ gives $x=\log(2u)$; if $u\ge\tfrac12$ then $1-\tfrac12e^{-x}=u$ gives $x=-\log(2(1-u))$.

For $u=0.2$: $x=\log0.4\approx-0.916$. For $u=0.9$: $x=-\log0.2\approx1.609$.

parts.text: Let $(U_1,V_1),\dots,(U_N,V_N)$ be i.i.d. uniform on the unit square, $I_i=\mathbf 1\{U_i^2+V_i^2\le1\}$ and $\hat\pi=\frac4N\sum_{i=1}^NI_i$. Show that $\hat\pi$ is unbiased for $\pi$ and that $\Var(\hat\pi)=\pi(4-\pi)/N$. How large must $N$ be for the standard error of $\hat\pi$ to be at most $0.001$?

markingScheme.step: $I_i$ is Bernoulli$(p)$ with $p=\pi/4$, so $\Var(I_i)=p(1-p)$ and by independence $\Var(\hat\pi)=\frac{16}{N}p(1-p)$

parts.modelAnswer:
The pair $(U_i,V_i)$ is uniform on the unit square, which has area $1$, so $\E[I_i]=\Prob(U_i^2+V_i^2\le1)=\pi/4=:p$. Hence $\E[\hat\pi]=\frac4N\cdot Np=\pi$, so $\hat\pi$ is unbiased.

$I_i\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p)$ with variance $p(1-p)$, and the $I_i$ are independent, so
$$\Var(\hat\pi)=\frac{16}{N^{2}}\cdot Np(1-p)=\frac{16}{N}\cdot\frac\pi4\Big(1-\frac\pi4\Big)=\frac{\pi(4-\pi)}{N}.$$
We need $\sqrt{\pi(4-\pi)/N}\le0.001$, i.e. $N\ge\pi(4-\pi)/10^{-6}\approx2.697\times10^{6}$, so about $2.7$ million points. $\blacksquare$

parts.text: Let $p$ be a target density, $q$ a proposal density with $q(x)>0$ whenever $p(x)g(x)\ne0$, and $w(x)=p(x)/q(x)$. (i) Prove the importance sampling identity $\E_q[w(X)g(X)]=\E_p[g(X)]$. (ii) Suppose only $\tilde p=cp$ is known (with $c>0$ unknown) and let $\tilde w=\tilde p/q$, $X_1,\dots,X_N\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}q$. Show that $\sum_i\tilde w(X_i)g(X_i)\big/\sum_i\tilde w(X_i)\to\E_p[g(X)]$ almost surely as $N\to\infty$, assuming $\E_p|g|<\infty$.

markingScheme.step: (ii) Strong law of large numbers: $\frac1N\sum\tilde wg\to\E_q[\tilde wg]=c\,\E_p[g]$ and $\frac1N\sum\tilde w\to\E_q[\tilde w]=c$
(ii) Ratio of the two limits (continuous mapping, $c>0$) is $\E_p[g]$

parts.modelAnswer:
(i) Using the support condition,
$$\E_q[w(X)g(X)]=\int\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}g(x)\,q(x)\,dx=\int g(x)p(x)\,dx=\E_p[g(X)].$$
(ii) Note $\tilde w=cw$. By the identity in (i), $\E_q[\tilde wg]=c\,\E_p[g]$ (finite since $\E_p|g|<\infty$) and, taking $g\equiv1$, $\E_q[\tilde w]=c$. By the strong law of large numbers,
$$\frac1N\sum_i\tilde w(X_i)g(X_i)\to c\,\E_p[g],\qquad\frac1N\sum_i\tilde w(X_i)\to c\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Since $c>0$ the ratio of the two averages, which equals $\sum_i\tilde wg/\sum_i\tilde w$, converges almost surely to $c\E_p[g]/c=\E_p[g]$. $\blacksquare$

parts.text: Four draws $x_1,\dots,x_4$ from a proposal $q$ have unnormalised importance weights $(1,2,3,2)$ and values $g(x_i)=(0,1,2,3)$. Compute the self-normalised importance sampling estimate of $\E_p[g]$ and the effective sample size $(\sum_i\tilde w_i)^2/\sum_i\tilde w_i^2$.
parts.modelAnswer:
$\sum\tilde w_i=1+2+3+2=8$ and $\sum\tilde w_ig_i=0+2+6+6=14$, so the estimate is $14/8=1.75$.

$\sum\tilde w_i^2=1+4+9+4=18$, so ESS $=64/18=32/9\approx3.556$, less than the nominal $4$ draws because the weights are unequal.

questions.title: Markov chains, Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling
questions.text: This question concerns the theory behind MCMC. All state spaces are finite unless stated otherwise.

parts.text: A Markov chain on $\{1,2,3\}$ has transition matrix $P=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2&0\\1/4&1/2&1/4\\0&1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}$. (i) Compute the two-step probabilities $P^2(1,3)$ and $P^2(2,2)$, and show that the chain is regular. (ii) A distribution $\pi$ satisfies detailed balance if $\pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_jP_{ji}$ for all $i,j$. Prove that detailed balance implies $\pi P=\pi$, and use it to find the stationary distribution of this chain.

markingScheme.step: (i) Shows every entry of $P^2$ is positive, so $P$ is regular
(ii) Sums detailed balance over $i$ and uses $\sum_iP_{ji}=1$ to get $(\pi P)_j=\pi_j$

parts.modelAnswer:
**(i)** Conditioning on the intermediate state, $P^2(i,j)=\sum_mP(i,m)P(m,j)$. Then
$$P^2(1,3)=\tfrac12\cdot0+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14+0\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac18,\qquad P^2(2,2)=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12+\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac12.$$
Computing all entries gives $P^2=\begin{pmatrix}3/8&1/2&1/8\\1/4&1/2&1/4\\1/8&1/2&3/8\end{pmatrix}$, all positive, so $P$ is regular.

**(ii)** Summing $\pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_jP_{ji}$ over $i$,
$$(\pi P)_j=\sum_i\pi_iP_{ij}=\sum_i\pi_jP_{ji}=\pi_j\sum_iP_{ji}=\pi_j,$$
because the rows of $P$ sum to $1$. Hence $\pi P=\pi$. $\blacksquare$

For this chain: $\pi_1P_{12}=\pi_2P_{21}$ gives $\tfrac12\pi_1=\tfrac14\pi_2$, so $\pi_2=2\pi_1$; $\pi_2P_{23}=\pi_3P_{32}$ gives $\tfrac14\pi_2=\tfrac12\pi_3$, so $\pi_3=\pi_1$. Normalising, $\pi=(\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac14)$. (Since the chain is regular, this is the unique stationary distribution.)

parts.text: Let $\pi$ be a distribution on a finite state space, $q(x,y)$ a proposal and $\alpha(x,y)=\min\Big\{1,\dfrac{\pi(y)q(y,x)}{\pi(x)q(x,y)}\Big\}$ the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability. For $x\ne y$ the chain moves from $x$ to $y$ with probability $K(x,y)=q(x,y)\alpha(x,y)$. Prove that $\pi(x)K(x,y)=\pi(y)K(y,x)$, so that $\pi$ is stationary.

markingScheme.step: This expression is symmetric in $x\leftrightarrow y$, so it equals $\pi(y)K(y,x)$
Concludes detailed balance holds and invokes part (a)(ii) for stationarity

parts.text: The target is $\tilde\pi(x)\propto x$ on $\{1,2,3\}$. The proposal moves to $x-1$ or $x+1$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each; a proposal outside $\{1,2,3\}$ is rejected (the chain stays). Find the acceptance probabilities, write the full transition matrix of the Metropolis-Hastings chain, and verify detailed balance for the pair of states $(2,3)$.
parts.modelAnswer:
Because the proposal is symmetric, $\alpha(x,y)=\min\{1,\tilde\pi(y)/\tilde\pi(x)\}$: $\alpha(1,2)=\min\{1,2\}=1$, $\alpha(2,1)=\tfrac12$, $\alpha(2,3)=\min\{1,\tfrac32\}=1$, $\alpha(3,2)=\tfrac23$.

Off-diagonal entries are $\tfrac12\alpha$: $P_{12}=\tfrac12$, $P_{21}=\tfrac14$, $P_{23}=\tfrac12$, $P_{32}=\tfrac13$, and $P_{13}=P_{31}=0$. Diagonals make rows sum to $1$ (rejected proposals stay put): $P_{11}=\tfrac12$, $P_{22}=\tfrac14$, $P_{33}=\tfrac23$. So
$$P=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2&0\\1/4&1/4&1/2\\0&1/3&2/3\end{pmatrix}.$$
The normalised target is $\pi=(\tfrac16,\tfrac26,\tfrac36)$. Then $\pi_2P_{23}=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac16$ and $\pi_3P_{32}=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac16$, so detailed balance holds.

parts.text: A Gibbs sampler targets $(X,Y)$ bivariate normal with zero means, unit variances and correlation $\rho\in(-1,1)$, with density $p(x,y)\propto\exp\Big\{-\dfrac{x^2-2\rho xy+y^2}{2(1-\rho^2)}\Big\}$. Derive the full conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y=y$.

markingScheme.step: Keeps only the terms involving $x$: $p(x\mid y)\propto\exp\{-(x^2-2\rho xy)/(2(1-\rho^2))\}$
Completes the square: $x^2-2\rho xy=(x-\rho y)^2-\rho^2y^2$ and drops the constant

parts.modelAnswer:
As a function of $x$, with $y$ fixed,
$$p(x\mid y)\propto\exp\Big\{-\frac{x^2-2\rho xy}{2(1-\rho^2)}\Big\}=\exp\Big\{-\frac{(x-\rho y)^2-\rho^2y^2}{2(1-\rho^2)}\Big\}\propto\exp\Big\{-\frac{(x-\rho y)^2}{2(1-\rho^2)}\Big\},$$
since $\rho^2y^2$ does not involve $x$. This is the kernel of $\mathcal N(\rho y,\,1-\rho^2)$, so $X\mid Y=y\sim\mathcal N(\rho y,1-\rho^2)$ (and symmetrically for $Y\mid X$).

parts.text: The $x$-draws of this Gibbs sampler, once stationary, form an AR(1) sequence with autocorrelation $\phi^{k}$ at lag $k$, where $\phi=\rho^{2}$. Show that the integrated autocorrelation time is $\tau=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\phi^{k}=\dfrac{1+\phi}{1-\phi}$, and compute the effective sample size $N/\tau$ for $N=2000$ draws and $\rho=0.8$.
parts.modelAnswer:
Since $|\phi|=\rho^2<1$, $\sum_{k\ge1}\phi^k=\phi/(1-\phi)$, so
$$\tau=1+\frac{2\phi}{1-\phi}=\frac{1-\phi+2\phi}{1-\phi}=\frac{1+\phi}{1-\phi}.\ \blacksquare$$
For $\rho=0.8$, $\phi=0.64$ and $\tau=1.64/0.36\approx4.556$. The effective sample size is $N/\tau=2000\times0.36/1.64\approx439$.

questions.title: Model comparison, Laplace approximation and variational Bayes
questions.text: This question is about comparing models and approximating posteriors.

parts.text: Observe $y=7$ successes in $n=10$ trials. Model $M_0$: $y\sim\text{Bin}(10,\tfrac12)$. Model $M_1$: $y\mid\theta\sim\text{Bin}(10,\theta)$ with $\theta\sim\text{Unif}(0,1)$. Compute both marginal likelihoods, the Bayes factor $B_{01}=p(y\mid M_0)/p(y\mid M_1)$, and the posterior probability of $M_0$ if the prior model probabilities are equal. (Use $B(8,4)=1/1320$.)
parts.modelAnswer:
Under $M_0$: $p(y\mid M_0)=\binom{10}{7}(1/2)^{10}=120/1024\approx0.1172$.

Under $M_1$ we integrate out $\theta$:
$$p(y\mid M_1)=\binom{10}{7}\int_0^1\theta^{7}(1-\theta)^{3}\,d\theta=120\,B(8,4)=\frac{120}{1320}=\frac1{11}\approx0.0909.$$
The Bayes factor is $B_{01}=\dfrac{120/1024}{1/11}=\dfrac{1320}{1024}=\dfrac{165}{128}\approx1.289$. With equal prior probabilities the posterior odds equal $B_{01}$, so
$$\Prob(M_0\mid y)=\frac{B_{01}}{1+B_{01}}=\frac{165}{293}\approx0.563.$$
The evidence slightly favours $M_0$: the diffuse prior in $M_1$ is penalised by the marginal likelihood.

parts.text: Let the posterior of $\theta$ be $\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\alpha,\beta>1$. Derive the Laplace approximation: find the mode $\hat\theta$ and the approximating variance $\hat\sigma^2=\big(-\ell''(\hat\theta)\big)^{-1}$, where $\ell$ is the log posterior density. Evaluate it for $\text{Beta}(8,4)$ and compare the variance with the exact posterior variance.

markingScheme.step: Log density up to a constant: $\ell(\theta)=(\alpha-1)\log\theta+(\beta-1)\log(1-\theta)$

parts.modelAnswer:
Up to a constant, $\ell(\theta)=(\alpha-1)\log\theta+(\beta-1)\log(1-\theta)$ and
$$\ell'(\theta)=\frac{\alpha-1}{\theta}-\frac{\beta-1}{1-\theta}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \hat\theta=\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha+\beta-2}.$$
Then $\ell''(\theta)=-\dfrac{\alpha-1}{\theta^{2}}-\dfrac{\beta-1}{(1-\theta)^{2}}$. At the mode, $1-\hat\theta=\dfrac{\beta-1}{\alpha+\beta-2}$, so
$$-\ell''(\hat\theta)=\frac{(\alpha+\beta-2)^2}{\alpha-1}+\frac{(\alpha+\beta-2)^2}{\beta-1}=\frac{(\alpha+\beta-2)^3}{(\alpha-1)(\beta-1)}.$$
Hence $\theta\mid y\approx\mathcal N\big(\hat\theta,\hat\sigma^2\big)$ with $\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{(\alpha-1)(\beta-1)}{(\alpha+\beta-2)^3}$.

For $\text{Beta}(8,4)$: $\hat\theta=7/10=0.7$ and $\hat\sigma^2=7\cdot3/10^3=0.021$. The exact mean is $8/12\approx0.667$ and the exact variance is $\dfrac{8\cdot4}{12^2\cdot13}=\dfrac{32}{1872}\approx0.0171$. The approximation is centred at the mode rather than the mean and is a little too wide for this small sample; it improves as $\alpha+\beta$ grows.

parts.text:
For two observations and $S=3$ posterior draws $\theta^{(s)}$ the values $p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})$ are

| | $s=1$ | $s=2$ | $s=3$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $y_1$ | 0.2 | 0.4 | 0.6 |
| $y_2$ | 0.1 | 0.3 | 0.2 |

Compute $\text{lppd}=\sum_i\log\big(\frac1S\sum_sp(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})\big)$, the penalty $p_{\text{WAIC}}=\sum_i\operatorname{Var}_s\big[\log p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})\big]$ (sample variance, divisor $S-1$) and $\text{WAIC}=-2(\text{lppd}-p_{\text{WAIC}})$.

markingScheme.step: Variance of the three log values for each observation, $\approx0.3086$ each

parts.modelAnswer:
Observation 1 has mean density $0.4$, observation 2 has $0.2$, so $\text{lppd}=\log0.4+\log0.2=-0.9163-1.6094=-2.5257$.

Observation 1: the log values are $\log0.2,\log0.4,\log0.6=-1.6094,-0.9163,-0.5108$ with mean $-1.0122$ and deviations $-0.5973,\,0.0959,\,0.5014$. Their sum of squares is $0.3567+0.0092+0.2514=0.6173$, so the sample variance is $0.3086$. Observation 2: $\log0.1,\log0.3,\log0.2=-2.3026,-1.2040,-1.6094$ are $\log 0.1+\{\log1,\log3,\log2\}$, while observation 1 gives $\log0.2+\{\log1,\log2,\log3\}$: the same three numbers up to order and a common shift, so the sample variance is again $0.3086$.

So $p_{\text{WAIC}}=0.6173$ and
$$\text{WAIC}=-2(-2.5257-0.6173)=6.286.$$

parts.text: For a model $p(y,\theta)$ and any density $q(\theta)$ define $\text{ELBO}(q)=\E_q[\log p(y,\theta)]-\E_q[\log q(\theta)]$. Prove that $\log p(y)=\text{ELBO}(q)+\operatorname{KL}\big(q\,\|\,p(\cdot\mid y)\big)$, and deduce that maximising the ELBO over a family of $q$ is the same as minimising the KL divergence to the posterior.

markingScheme.step: Writes $\log p(y)=\log p(y,\theta)-\log p(\theta\mid y)$ for any $\theta$
Takes $\E_q$ of both sides (the left side does not depend on $\theta$)
Adds and subtracts $\E_q[\log q]$ to obtain $\text{ELBO}(q)+\operatorname{KL}(q\|p(\cdot\mid y))$
$\operatorname{KL}\ge0$ so $\text{ELBO}\le\log p(y)$; since $\log p(y)$ is fixed, maximising ELBO minimises KL

questions.title: Nonparametric Bayes: CRP, stick-breaking, DP and GP
questions.text: This question is about nonparametric Bayesian models. Throughout, $\alpha>0$ is the concentration parameter and $G_0$ the base measure.

parts.text: In a Chinese restaurant process with concentration $\alpha=2$, customer $n+1$ joins an occupied table with probability proportional to its current size $n_k$ and opens a new table with probability proportional to $\alpha$ (the normaliser is $n+\alpha$). Find the probability that the first four customers sit as $\{1,2\},\{3\},\{4\}$, and the probability that customer 5 then opens a new table.

markingScheme.step: Customer 1 opens a table (prob. $1$); customer 2 joins it with prob. $\frac{1}{1+2}=\frac13$
Customer 3 opens a new table with prob. $\frac{2}{2+2}=\frac12$; customer 4 with prob. $\frac{2}{3+2}=\frac25$; product $=\frac1{15}$
Customer 5 opens a new table with prob. $\frac{2}{4+2}=\frac13$

parts.modelAnswer:
Customer 1 sits at a new table with probability $1$. Customer 2 joins it with probability $\frac{1}{1+2}=\frac13$. Customer 3 starts a new table with probability $\frac{2}{2+2}=\frac12$. Customer 4 starts another new table with probability $\frac{2}{3+2}=\frac25$. The probability of this seating is
$$1\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac25=\frac1{15}.$$
Customer 5 opens a new table with probability $\frac{2}{4+2}=\frac13$ (regardless of the table sizes).

parts.text: Let $K_n$ be the number of occupied tables after $n$ customers in a Chinese restaurant process with concentration $\alpha$. Prove that $\E[K_n]=\sum_{i=1}^n\dfrac{\alpha}{\alpha+i-1}$ and evaluate it for $\alpha=2$, $n=4$.

markingScheme.step: Defines $Z_i=\mathbf 1\{\text{customer } i\text{ opens a new table}\}$ so $K_n=\sum_iZ_i$
Shows $\Prob(Z_i=1)=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+i-1}$ (the $i$th customer sees $i-1$ people already seated)
Linearity of expectation gives the formula

parts.modelAnswer:
Let $Z_i=1$ if customer $i$ opens a new table and $0$ otherwise, so $K_n=\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i$. When customer $i$ arrives, $i-1$ customers are seated, so the probability of a new table is $\Prob(Z_i=1)=\alpha/(\alpha+i-1)$, whatever the seating so far. By linearity of expectation,
$$\E[K_n]=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+i-1}.\ \blacksquare$$
For $\alpha=2$, $n=4$: $\E[K_4]=\frac22+\frac23+\frac24+\frac25=1+\frac23+\frac12+\frac25=\frac{77}{30}\approx2.567$.

parts.text: In the stick-breaking construction, $V_k\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\text{Beta}(1,\alpha)$ and $\pi_k=V_k\prod_{j<k}(1-V_j)$. Prove that $\E[\pi_k]=\dfrac1{1+\alpha}\Big(\dfrac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}\Big)^{k-1}$, evaluate $\E[\pi_1],\E[\pi_2],\E[\pi_3]$ for $\alpha=2$, and prove that $\sum_{k\ge1}\pi_k=1$ almost surely.

markingScheme.step: The product is non-increasing with expectation $(\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha})^K\to0$, so it tends to $0$ a.s. and the weights sum to $1$

parts.modelAnswer:
Since $V_1,V_2,\dots$ are independent,
$$\E[\pi_k]=\E[V_k]\prod_{j<k}\E[1-V_j].$$
For $V\sim\text{Beta}(1,\alpha)$, $\E[V]=\frac{1}{1+\alpha}$ and $\E[1-V]=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}$, so $\E[\pi_k]=\frac1{1+\alpha}\big(\frac\alpha{1+\alpha}\big)^{k-1}$. For $\alpha=2$: $\E[\pi_1]=\frac13$, $\E[\pi_2]=\frac13\cdot\frac23=\frac29$, $\E[\pi_3]=\frac13\cdot\frac49=\frac4{27}$.

For the total mass, show by induction that $\sum_{k\le K}\pi_k=1-\prod_{j\le K}(1-V_j)$: true for $K=1$; and $1-\prod_{j\le K}(1-V_j)+V_{K+1}\prod_{j\le K}(1-V_j)=1-\prod_{j\le K+1}(1-V_j)$. The product $\prod_{j\le K}(1-V_j)$ is non-negative and non-increasing in $K$, so it converges almost surely, and its expectation is $\big(\frac\alpha{1+\alpha}\big)^K\to0$. A non-negative limit with expectation $0$ is $0$ almost surely (Fatou / monotone convergence), hence $\sum_{k\ge1}\pi_k=1$ a.s. $\blacksquare$

parts.text: A function $f$ has a Gaussian process prior $f\sim\mathcal{GP}(0,k)$ with $k(x,x')=\exp\{-(x-x')^2/2\}$. We observe $y=f(0)+\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,0.25)$ independent of $f$, and the single observation is $y=1.2$. Derive the posterior mean and variance of $f(1)$ (3 decimal places).

markingScheme.step: $(y,f(1))$ is jointly Gaussian with zero mean, $\operatorname{Var}(y)=1.25$, $\operatorname{Cov}(y,f(1))=e^{-1/2}\approx0.6065$, $\operatorname{Var}f(1)=1$

parts.modelAnswer:
The vector $(y,f(1))$ is jointly Gaussian with zero mean and covariance
$$\begin{pmatrix}k(0,0)+0.25&k(0,1)\\k(0,1)&k(1,1)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1.25&e^{-1/2}\\e^{-1/2}&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad e^{-1/2}\approx0.6065.$$
Conditioning a bivariate Gaussian,
$$\E[f(1)\mid y]=\frac{e^{-1/2}}{1.25}\,y=\frac{0.6065}{1.25}\times1.2\approx0.582,$$
$$\Var(f(1)\mid y)=1-\frac{e^{-1}}{1.25}=1-\frac{0.3679}{1.25}\approx0.706.$$
The observation pulls the prediction at $x=1$ towards $y$, and reduces its variance from $1$ to $0.706$.

parts.text: A random measure $G\sim\text{DP}(\alpha,G_0)$ is defined by requiring that, for every finite measurable partition $A_1,\dots,A_m$ of the space, $(G(A_1),\dots,G(A_m))\sim\text{Dirichlet}(\alpha G_0(A_1),\dots,\alpha G_0(A_m))$. For a set $A$ with $p=G_0(A)\in(0,1)$, prove that $\E[G(A)]=p$ and $\Var[G(A)]=\dfrac{p(1-p)}{\alpha+1}$.

markingScheme.step: Applies the definition to the partition $\{A,A^c\}$: $(G(A),G(A^c))\sim\text{Dirichlet}(\alpha p,\alpha(1-p))$
Marginal of a two-component Dirichlet: $G(A)\sim\text{Beta}(\alpha p,\alpha(1-p))$

parts.modelAnswer:
Apply the definition to the partition $\{A,A^c\}$: $(G(A),G(A^c))\sim\text{Dirichlet}(\alpha p,\alpha(1-p))$, so the marginal is $G(A)\sim\text{Beta}(\alpha p,\alpha(1-p))$. For $\text{Beta}(u,v)$ the mean is $u/(u+v)$ and the variance is $uv/((u+v)^2(u+v+1))$. Here $u+v=\alpha$, so
$$\E[G(A)]=\frac{\alpha p}{\alpha}=p,\qquad\Var[G(A)]=\frac{\alpha p\cdot\alpha(1-p)}{\alpha^2(\alpha+1)}=\frac{p(1-p)}{\alpha+1}.\ \blacksquare$$
So $G_0$ is the prior mean of $G$, and $\alpha$ controls how tightly $G$ concentrates around $G_0$.
